title: REST APIs
body:
Interview prep note. See [[API]] for the course-notes version of the same term.

## Core Facts to Know

- An [[API]] is a contract between a client and a server.
- The point of an API is that the backend can be rewritten without changing the contract.
- [[REST]] organizes endpoints around nouns (resources), not verb-named endpoints.
- A resource is the noun, e.g. `reviews`, `products`, `users`.
- An [[Endpoint]] is one specific URL the server has a handler for.
- Endpoints are defined and hosted on the server.
- Request and response bodies are usually [[JSON]].
- The client builds the request body; the server builds the response body.
- [[Authentication]] is proving who you are.
- [[Authorization]] is whether that identity is allowed to do this specific thing.
- Credentials are presented by the client and checked by the server.
- [[Rate Limiting]] is enforced on the server and reported with 429 Too Many Requests.
- [[Pagination]] is requested by the client and fulfilled by the server.
- [[API Versioning]] keeps an old contract alive while a new one rolls out.
- [[Fetch]] returns a [[Promise]].
- Asynchronicity means other JS keeps running while the response is awaited.
- The thing that keeps other JS running is the [[Event Loop]].
- [[Client-Side Rendering]] builds the DOM on your machine from fetched JSON.
- [[Server-Side Rendering]] builds the HTML on their machine before it reaches you.
- Third-party API requests originate on your machine but are handled by a third party's machine.
- A [[Webhook]] is initiated by their machine, not yours.
- Webhooks are server-to-server, so they arrive at a server you control, never at your browser.

## Core analogy: A restaurant menu and kitchen

You (the [[Client]]/frontend) don't walk into the kitchen and cook the food yourself. You read a menu (the API contract) and hand your order (a request) to a waiter (the API). The waiter takes it to the kitchen (the backend/server, which may involve a database), and brings back a plate (the response) in a format you both agreed on ahead of time. The point of an API is that the kitchen can be completely renovated without changing the menu — frontend and backend evolve independently as long as the contract holds.

## REST API concepts, mapped

| Restaurant term | API term | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| A specific menu item | Endpoint, e.g. `/api/reviews/123` | Defined and hosted on **their machine** (the server's router) |
| The noun the menu is organized around | Resource (`reviews`, `products`, `users`) — REST is nouns + HTTP methods, not verb-named endpoints | Defined by **their machine's** API design |
| The written order slip and the plate's contents | Request/response body, usually JSON | Built by **your machine** (request), built by **their machine** (response) |
| Showing your membership card before ordering | Authentication (API keys, OAuth tokens, session cookies) — distinct from *authorization*, which is whether your membership tier allows this specific order | Card presented by **your machine**, checked by **their machine** |
| The kitchen only accepts so many orders per minute | Rate limits (429 Too Many Requests) | Enforced on **their machine** |
| Food brought out in courses instead of all at once | Pagination (`?page=2&limit=20`) | Requested by **your machine**, fulfilled by **their machine** |
| Old menu kept available for regulars while a new one rolls out | Versioning (`/v1/reviews`, `/v2/reviews`) | Maintained on **their machine** |

The methods themselves (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) are covered in [[HTTP Requests]].

## Where this shows up in frontend development specifically

| Restaurant term | Concept | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| The waiter-calling mechanism | `fetch` / `XMLHttpRequest` / Axios — construct a request, send it, get a `Promise` back | **Your machine** — JS engine calling into the browser's networking layer |
| Not freezing at your table while food is prepared | Asynchronicity — other JS keeps running via the event loop while awaiting the response | **Your machine** — the JS engine's event loop |
| Either you assemble the plate yourself from raw ingredients, or the kitchen sends it already plated | Client-side rendering (browser builds DOM from fetched JSON, e.g. a [[React]] SPA) vs. server-side rendering (server sends pre-built HTML) | CSR happens on **your machine**; SSR happens on **their machine**, before the page even reaches you |
| Other restaurants your code has to place orders with, using their menu | Third-party APIs/integrations — Google Analytics, Tag Management Systems, client integrations | Requests originate on **your machine**, handled by a **third party's machine**, not the same one you're logged into |
| The kitchen calls you when your order's ready, instead of you asking repeatedly | Webhooks | Initiated by **their machine**, received by a server **you** control (not your browser — webhooks are server-to-server) |

Practical JS for all of this: [[Fetch]], [[Async Functions]], [[Parallel Fetches]], and [[Express]] for building the server side of the contract.
